title: Multi-Objective Learning for Diffusion Models: A Statistical Theory under Semi-Supervised Learning
claim: Fit lightweight specialists on scarce paired data, then distill them via pseudo-labeled data into a generalist, cutting sample complexity.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right; data panels feed middle stage into generalist panel
description: A wide left-to-right diagram in three color-coded rounded panels. At left, a blue box shows limited paired data for Objectives 1 through K, with condition images (masked faces) mapped to target faces. Below it, an orange box shows abundant condition-only data as stacks of small labeled tokens for each objective. In the middle, a teal box titled Semi-supervised MOL has two steps: train small specialists h_1 to h_K (neural-net icons), then generate pseudo-paired face images. Arrows lead right. A blue arrow labeled 'labeled data only' skips the middle stage, and a second arrow carries labeled plus pseudo data. At right, a purple box shows the large generalist, a U-Net denoising from noise x_T to x_0. Below it are a theory box comparing sample complexity bounds and an applications box with image generation and robot arms.
caption: Semi-supervised multi-objective learning for conditional diffusion models. Given limited paired data $\{(x_i^k,y_i^k)\}_{i=1}^n \stackrel{i.i.d.}\sim \P_k$ and abundant condition-only data $\{\widetilde y_i^k\}_{i=1}^N \stackrel{i.i.d.}\sim \P_k^Y$ for each objective $k$, we first train lightweight specialists $\widehat h_k \in \mathcal H_k$ and use them to generate pseudo-paired data. A large diffusion generalist in class $\mathcal F$ is then trained on labeled and pseudo-labeled data. This reduces the paired-sample complexity from scaling with the generalist complexity $C_\mathcal F$ to scaling with the specialist complexity $C_\mathcal H$ where $C_\mathcal H \ll C_\mathcal F $.
abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly used as powerful conditional generators, yet real deployments often involve multiple target distributions arising from different tasks, e.g., diverse prompt domains in text-to-image generation, or multiple environments in robotics with diffusion policies. This naturally leads to a multi-objective learning (MOL) problem. A key challenge is that achieving good Pareto trade-offs can require a generalist model class with substantially larger capacity than what suffices for solving any individual task, thereby increasing statistical cost since sample complexity typically scales with the model complexity. To reconcile this, we develop a principled MOL framework for diffusion models with limited data: a semi-supervised regime where paired (labeled) samples are scarce, but (unlabeled) condition data are abundant. We propose a two-stage training procedure that first fits lightweight specialist models from limited paired data, and then distills them into a generalist model by generating pseudo-samples. We establish generalization bounds showing that the required number of paired samples only depends on the complexity of the specialist model classes. We further extend the theory to diffusion policies for sequential decision making to account for distribution shift in on-policy rollouts. Extensive experiments on robotic control and image restoration tasks are conducted to verify our theoretical results.
